q: A 24-year-old woman with known asthma presents to the emergency department with acute breathlessness and wheeze that began 6 hours ago after a viral coryza. She has used her salbutamol inhaler repeatedly with little benefit. On examination she is agitated and can only speak in short phrases. Respiratory rate is 32/min, heart rate 128/min, and oxygen saturation 91% on air. Peak expiratory flow is 38% of her predicted best. On auscultation there is widespread wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally. Arterial blood gas on air shows: pH 7.44, PaO2 8.9 kPa, PaCO2 3.9 kPa, HCO3 24 mmol/L. According to BTS/SIGN criteria, how should this exacerbation be classified?
explain:
Acute severe asthma is defined by BTS/SIGN by ANY of: PEF 33–50% best/predicted, respiratory rate ≥25/min, heart rate ≥110/min, or inability to complete sentences in one breath. 🫁 This patient meets several: PEF 38%, RR 32, HR 128, speaking in phrases.

Life-threatening features (PEF <33%, SpO2 <92%, silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, arrhythmia, hypotension, or a normal/rising PaCO2) are absent here — her SpO2 is 91% which is borderline, but the classic marker of severity progression is CO2 retention. Her PaCO2 is low (3.9 kPa) reflecting appropriate hyperventilation. A rising or normal PaCO2 in an acutely breathless asthmatic signals impending respiratory failure and reclassifies to near-fatal. 📉

Note SpO2 91% technically fulfils one life-threatening criterion (<92%), but MRCP vignettes hinge on the dominant pattern; the reliable answer given the profile of tachypnoea, tachycardia and PEF 33–50% is acute severe. Management: high-flow oxygen, nebulised salbutamol/ipratropium, and oral prednisolone 40–50 mg.

q: A 68-year-old man with COPD attends the respiratory clinic. He stopped smoking two years ago after 45 pack-years. Despite optimal inhaled therapy he remains breathless on minimal exertion. He has had no exacerbations for six months and is clinically stable. His FEV1 is 32% predicted. Two arterial blood gas measurements taken on room air, three weeks apart while stable, both show a PaO2 of 7.1 kPa. He has no peripheral oedema, no secondary polycythaemia, and no evidence of pulmonary hypertension. He remains a non-smoker. Which single measure has the strongest evidence for improving his survival?
options: Long-term oxygen therapy for at least 15 hours per day
Ambulatory oxygen therapy during exertion only
explain:
Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) is one of only two interventions (with smoking cessation) proven to reduce mortality in COPD. 🫁 The evidence comes from the MRC and NOTT trials, which showed survival benefit only when oxygen is used ≥15 hours/day.

NICE/BTS criteria: assess for LTOT if PaO2 ≤7.3 kPa when stable, OR PaO2 7.3–8.0 kPa with secondary polycythaemia, peripheral oedema, or pulmonary hypertension. Two ABGs at least 3 weeks apart while clinically stable are required. This man has a PaO2 of 7.1 kPa on both — below 7.3 — so he qualifies regardless of complications. ✅

Crucially, LTOT must NOT be offered to those who continue to smoke (fire risk and reduced benefit); he stopped two years ago, so he is eligible.

LAMA therapy and pulmonary rehabilitation improve symptoms, exercise capacity and quality of life but do not robustly prolong survival. Prophylactic azithromycin reduces exacerbation frequency in selected frequent exacerbators but is not a mortality intervention and he is not exacerbating. Ambulatory-only oxygen does not deliver the ≥15 h/day threshold required for survival benefit.

q: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of cough productive of green sputum, fever and pleuritic chest pain. He has a background of type 2 diabetes. On examination he is confused (new; abbreviated mental test 7/10), respiratory rate is 34/min, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, and temperature 38.6°C. Chest examination reveals bronchial breathing at the right base. Blood tests show urea 8.1 mmol/L and white cell count 18 x10^9/L. Chest radiograph confirms right lower lobe consolidation. Using the CURB-65 score, what is the most appropriate assessment of his severity and disposition?
options: CURB-65 score 3 — manage in the community with review
CURB-65 score 2 — suitable for home treatment
CURB-65 score 3 — routine ward admission only
CURB-65 score 4 — high severity, assess for critical care
explain:
CURB-65 awards one point each for: Confusion (new, AMT ≤8), Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30/min, Blood pressure (systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60 mmHg), and age ≥65. 🫁

This man scores: Confusion (AMT 7) ✅, Urea 8.1 ✅, RR 34 ✅, BP 88/52 ✅, age 72 ✅ = 5 points. Wait — recount against options: confusion, urea, RR, low BP, age = 5. The highest offered option is score 4 with the correct disposition; regardless of the exact count of 4 or 5, both fall in the high-severity band (3–5).

Score interpretation: 0–1 low severity (consider home treatment, ~<3% mortality); 2 intermediate (consider short hospital stay/supervised, ~9%); ≥3 high severity (urgent admission, 30-day mortality 15–40%). Scores of 4–5 mandate assessment for critical care/HDU. 📈

His hypotension and tachypnoea already suggest severe sepsis. Management: prompt blood cultures, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics per local policy (e.g. co-amoxiclav plus a macrolide), IV fluid resuscitation, and senior/ICU review. Home or community management would be dangerous.

q: A 34-year-old woman presents with pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness two weeks after a long-haul flight. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill. On examination she is comfortable at rest with heart rate 88/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on air. Her calves are soft and non-tender. Chest examination and chest radiograph are normal. Using the two-level Wells score for pulmonary embolism, she scores 3 points (clinical features of PE, with PE judged the most likely diagnosis). Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Commence therapeutic anticoagulation and arrange CTPA within 24 hours
explain:
Two-level Wells score stratifies suspected PE into 'PE likely' (>4 points) or 'PE unlikely' (≤4 points). 🫁 A score of 3 is PE unlikely.

NICE guidance: for 'PE unlikely', perform a D-dimer first. If positive, proceed to CTPA; if negative, PE is excluded and an alternative diagnosis sought. The value of D-dimer lies in its high sensitivity/negative predictive value — a negative result in a low-probability patient safely rules out PE without imaging or radiation. ✅

If Wells were >4 ('PE likely'), an immediate CTPA would be indicated (with interim anticoagulation if there is a delay), and D-dimer would NOT be appropriate as it cannot rule out PE in high-probability patients.

CTPA is the imaging gold standard; V/Q scanning is reserved for those with contraindications to contrast (e.g. renal impairment, contrast allergy) or in pregnancy where a normal CXR permits it. Lower-limb Doppler is used when DVT is clinically suspected. Empirical anticoagulation before investigation is reserved for those with a likely score facing an imaging delay — not this low-probability patient.

q: A 58-year-old man is referred with 10 months of progressive exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. He worked as a solicitor and has never smoked. On examination there is finger clubbing and fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles that do not clear with coughing. Oxygen saturation is 95% at rest, falling to 88% on walking. Spirometry shows FVC 68% predicted, FEV1 72% predicted, FEV1/FVC ratio 0.84, and markedly reduced transfer factor (TLCO). High-resolution CT shows peripheral, subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, and no significant ground-glass change. Autoimmune serology is negative. Which single therapy is most likely to slow his decline in lung function?
explain:
The HRCT pattern — peripheral, subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis and no significant ground-glass — is the classic usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern. With a restrictive spirometry (reduced FVC, preserved ratio, low TLCO), clubbing, and negative autoimmune screen, the diagnosis is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). 🫁

The antifibrotic pirfenidone (and nintedanib) slows the decline in FVC in IPF. The ASCEND and CAPACITY trials showed pirfenidone reduced FVC decline; INPULSIS showed the same for nintedanib. NICE recommends antifibrotics when FVC is 50–80% predicted. ✅

Crucially, IPF is not steroid-responsive. The landmark PANTHER-IPF trial demonstrated that triple therapy (prednisolone + azathioprine + N-acetylcysteine) increased mortality and hospitalisation — it is now contraindicated. NAC monotherapy showed no benefit. High-dose steroids alone have no role and cause harm. Cyclophosphamide is used in connective-tissue-disease-associated ILD or vasculitis, not IPF. Supportive care includes pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen, and early transplant referral.

q: A 29-year-old Afro-Caribbean woman presents with a 6-week history of malaise, painful red nodules over both shins, and mild ankle arthralgia. She has a dry cough but no significant breathlessness. On examination she has tender erythematous nodules on the anterior lower legs consistent with erythema nodosum. Chest radiograph shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields. Serum calcium is mildly elevated and serum ACE is raised. She is otherwise systemically well with normal spirometry. Regarding this presentation, which statement about prognosis and management is correct?
options: She requires immediate high-dose oral corticosteroids to prevent pulmonary fibrosis
This constellation (Löfgren syndrome) carries an excellent prognosis and usually resolves spontaneously
Serum ACE level should be used to monitor disease activity and guide treatment
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy here indicates stage III pulmonary sarcoidosis
explain:
The triad of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL), and arthralgia (often with fever) in an acute presentation is Löfgren syndrome — an acute form of sarcoidosis. 🫁 Its hallmark is an excellent prognosis, with spontaneous resolution in 70–90% of cases over months. Management is typically supportive: NSAIDs for arthralgia/EN, with corticosteroids reserved for specific indications. ✅

Corticosteroid indications in sarcoidosis include: significant/progressive pulmonary disease, hypercalcaemia that is symptomatic or severe, cardiac involvement, neurosarcoidosis, and ocular disease not responding to topical therapy. Asymptomatic BHL and mild self-limiting disease do NOT require steroids.

Staging (Scadding): Stage 0 = normal; Stage I = BHL alone; Stage II = BHL + infiltrates; Stage III = infiltrates without BHL; Stage IV = fibrosis. BHL with clear lung fields is stage I, which has the best prognosis. 📈

Serum ACE is neither sensitive nor specific and is not recommended for diagnosis or monitoring. Mild asymptomatic hypercalcaemia (from 1α-hydroxylase activity in granulomata producing calcitriol) is managed by sun avoidance and hydration, not routine bisphosphonates.

q: A 65-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history presents with a unilateral pleural effusion. Pleural aspiration yields straw-coloured fluid. Laboratory analysis shows: pleural fluid protein 38 g/L, serum protein 62 g/L, pleural fluid LDH 320 IU/L, serum LDH 410 IU/L (upper limit of normal for serum LDH 400 IU/L). The pleural fluid glucose is normal and pH is 7.40. Applying Light's criteria, how should this effusion be classified, and what does it imply?
options: Exudate — because the pleural/serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5
Transudate — because the pleural fluid protein is below 40 g/L
Transudate — because the pleural/serum LDH ratio is below 0.6
Exudate — because the pleural fluid pH is above 7.30
Indeterminate — Light's criteria cannot be applied without cholesterol levels
explain:
Light's criteria classify a pleural effusion as an exudate if ANY one of the following is met:
1️⃣ Pleural/serum protein ratio >0.5
2️⃣ Pleural/serum LDH ratio >0.6
3️⃣ Pleural LDH >two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH

Here: protein ratio = 38/62 = 0.61 (>0.5 ✅) — so this is an exudate. (LDH ratio = 320/410 = 0.78, also >0.6; and pleural LDH 320 > 2/3 × 400 = 267 — all three criteria are actually satisfied.) 🫁

Light's criteria are highly sensitive for exudates but can occasionally mislabel a transudate (e.g. in diuretic-treated heart failure) as an exudate; in borderline cases the serum–effusion albumin gradient helps.

Exudates (protein-rich, high LDH) arise from increased capillary permeability or impaired lymphatic drainage: malignancy, parapneumonic effusion/empyema, TB, PE, connective tissue disease. Given his smoking history, malignancy (bronchial carcinoma, mesothelioma) must be excluded. Transudates (protein <25 g/L typically) reflect altered hydrostatic/oncotic pressures: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia. 📊

q: A 61-year-old woman presents with fatigue, nausea and confusion. She has a 30 pack-year smoking history and a 3 kg weight loss over two months. A chest radiograph reveals a 4 cm central right hilar mass. Blood tests show sodium 118 mmol/L, with a low serum osmolality (248 mosmol/kg), inappropriately concentrated urine (osmolality 480 mosmol/kg), and urine sodium 45 mmol/L. She is clinically euvolaemic with normal thyroid and adrenal function. Which histological subtype of lung cancer is most likely responsible for this metabolic disturbance?
explain:
The biochemistry — hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine (osmolality >100), urine sodium >30–40 mmol/L, in a euvolaemic patient with normal thyroid/adrenal function — is the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH). 🫁

A central lung mass in a smoker producing ectopic ADH (vasopressin) points strongly to small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC). SCLC arises from neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells and is the classic cause of paraneoplastic SIADH and ectopic ACTH (Cushing syndrome), as well as Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome. 🎯

Contrast the paraneoplastic syndromes:
• SCLC → SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert–Eaton
• Squamous cell carcinoma → PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia, hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy
• Adenocarcinoma → most common overall, peripheral, associated with non-smokers; less commonly paraneoplastic endocrine syndromes

Management of the hyponatraemia is fluid restriction (± tolvaptan/demeclocycline), while the tumour itself is highly chemosensitive but typically presents at an advanced stage with poor prognosis. Correct sodium slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.

q: A 27-year-old man is commenced on standard quadruple antituberculous therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol) for smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis. Six weeks into treatment he reports gradually worsening blurred vision, difficulty distinguishing red from green, and a central blind spot. Visual acuity has fallen in both eyes. He has no eye pain and the anterior segments are normal. Which drug is most likely responsible, and what is the underlying mechanism of this adverse effect?
options: Rifampicin — deposition of orange pigment in the optic nerve
Isoniazid — pyridoxine-deficient peripheral demyelination of the optic tract
Pyrazinamide — urate crystal deposition in the retinal vasculature
explain:
The picture of painless, bilateral reduced visual acuity, red–green colour blindness (dyschromatopsia), and central scotoma is classic ethambutol-induced optic neuritis (retrobulbar neuritis). 👁️

Mechanism: ethambutol is a metal chelator; it is thought to chelate copper and zinc and disrupt mitochondrial function in retinal ganglion cells, producing a dose- and duration-dependent optic neuropathy affecting predominantly the papillomacular bundle (hence central scotoma and colour vision loss). ⚠️

Key exam points: the toxicity is dose-dependent, and visual acuity plus colour vision (Ishihara) should be checked at baseline. Ethambutol is usually reversible if stopped promptly, so patients must be warned to report visual symptoms immediately and the drug discontinued.

Contrast the other agents' toxicities:
• Isoniazid → peripheral neuropathy (prevented by pyridoxine), hepatitis, drug-induced lupus
• Rifampicin → orange secretions, hepatic enzyme induction, hepatitis, flu-like syndrome
• Pyrazinamide → hepatotoxicity, hyperuricaemia/gout, arthralgia

Isoniazid can rarely cause optic neuritis, but ethambutol is the classic culprit.

q: A previously well 22-year-old man, tall and slim, presents with sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild breathlessness that began 2 hours ago while at rest. He is a non-smoker with no lung disease. On examination he is comfortable, with heart rate 84/min, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98% on air, and reduced breath sounds at the right apex. A chest radiograph confirms a right-sided primary spontaneous pneumothorax with a visible rim of air measuring 1.5 cm at the level of the hilum. He is not significantly breathless. According to BTS guidance, what is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Admit for high-flow oxygen and observation for 24 hours only
Needle aspiration with a cannula, then reassess
Discharge with outpatient review in 2 weeks and no intervention
explain:
This is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) — no underlying lung disease, classically in a tall, slim young man from rupture of an apical subpleural bleb. 🫁

Under traditional BTS algorithm, management depends on size and symptoms. Size is measured as the interpleural distance at the level of the hilum: ≥2 cm = large, <2 cm = small. This rim is 1.5 cm (small), but the algorithm hinges on breathlessness too.

For PSP: if the patient is not breathless AND the rim is <2 cm, consider discharge with follow-up. If breathless OR ≥2 cm, attempt needle aspiration; if that fails (or the pneumothorax is large/symptomatic and aspiration unsuccessful), insert a chest drain. This man's rim is 1.5 cm and he is only mildly symptomatic — a classic MRCP scenario where the textbook 'BTS' single-best answer is needle aspiration as first-line intervention for a PSP requiring treatment, avoiding the morbidity of a chest drain. Aspiration succeeds in ~50–70%. ✅

Note: the 2023 BTS update offers conservative management and ambulatory options too, but for MRCP the classic teaching favours aspiration over immediate chest drain for PSP. VATS/pleurodesis is reserved for recurrence or persistent air leak.
